|editor3-first=Adrián|url-access=subscription }} == History == [[file: Mascara lambayeque ( museo de Sican).jpg|thumb|200px|Funerary mask from [[Batán Grande]] (Sican culture).]] === Language contact === Jolkesky (2016) notes that there are lexical similarities with the [[Trumai language|Trumai]], [[Arawak languages|Arawak]], [[Kandoshi language|Kandoshi]], [[Muniche language|Muniche]], [[Barbakoa languages|Barbakoa]], [[Cholon-Hibito languages|Cholon-Hibito]], [[Kechua languages|Kechua]], [[Mapudungun languages|Mapudungun]], [[Kanichana language|Kanichana]], and [[Kunza language|Kunza]] language families due to contact, also suggesting that similarities with Amazonian languages may be due to the early migration of Mochica speakers down the [[Marañón River|Marañón]] and [[Solimões]].{{cite thesis |last=Jolkesky |first=Marcelo Pinho de Valhery |title=Estudo arqueo-ecolinguístico das terras tropicais sul-americanas |date=2016 |type=Ph.D. dissertation |publisher=University of Brasília |url=http://www.etnolinguistica.org/tese:jolkesky-2016-arqueoecolinguistica |location=Brasília |edition=2}} == Documentation == === Colonial-era texts === The earliest published documentation of Mochica dates back to 1607 in {{lang|es|Rituale seu Manuale Peruanum}} (1607), written by [[Franciscans|Franciscan]] friar [[Luis Jerónimo de Oré]] (missionary, polyglot, later bishop of [[Concepción, Chile|Concepción]] in Chile), containing some Mochica sentences of unknown origin. However, a 1582 manuscript believed to be hosted at the Archiepiscopal Archive of Trujillo titled ''Gobierno de los situmas antes de los señores yngas comenzasen a reinar, y trata quienes fueron y mandaron en aqueste valle, Cañaribamba'' purported to contain information in [[Cañari language|Cañari]], an extinct and poorly known language of Ecuador, has Mochica texts which were copied and published elsewhere but assumed to be of Cañari origin. Following that, in 1644, the diocesan priest and parish [[vicar]] of [[Reque District|Reque]] {{Ill|Fernando de la Carrera Daza|es|Fernando de la Carrera Daza}} published the {{lang|es|{{Ill|Arte de la lengua yunga|es|Arte de la lengua yunga}}}} ('Art of the Yunga Language'), the only known colonial grammar of this language, is one of the primary sources of data on Mochica, including a descriptive grammar, religious texts, and general information about the Lambayeque region. A document known as the "plan" of [[Bishop of Trujillo]] [[Baltasar Jaime Martínez Compañón]] in his [[Codex Martínez Compañón]], a general account of life in 18th-century Peru, contains a 43-word list in Mochica.{{Cite book |last=Urban|first=Matthias|url=https://core.ac.uk/download/pdf/304709916.pdf|title=Lost languages of the Peruvian north coast|date=2019|publisher=Gebr. Mann Verlag|isbn=978-3-7861-2826-7|series=Estudios Indiana|location=Berlin|pages=73–96|oclc=on1090545680}} === 19th-20th century texts === Towards the end of Mochica's existence as a native language in the 19th century, various scholars such as [[Adolf Bastian]], the German physician and philologist {{ill|Ernst Middendorf|lt=Ernst W. Middendorf|de|Ernst Wilhelm Middendorf}}, [[Walter Lehmann (ethnologist)|Walter Lehmann]], [[Federico Villarreal]], and [[Hans Heinrich Brüning]] documented Mochica, most notably Middendorf, who authored the other primary source on Mochica, a grammar incorporating some elements of Carrera's work, but also some new content.{{Cite book |last1=Adelaar|first1=Willem F. H.|url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/9780511486852/type/book|title=The Languages of the Andes|last2=Muysken|first2=Pieter C.|date=2004-06-10|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0-521-36275-7|edition=1|doi=10.1017/cbo9780511486852.005}} Following the death of the last fluent speakers, a number of new sources of documentation were published, by Konrad Huber (1953), who collected data from 1943-47, also including an unpublished wordlist by Rafael Quesquén,{{Cite journal |last=Huber |first=Konrad |date=1953 |title=Contribution à la langue mučik. |url=https://www.persee.fr/doc/jsa_0037-9174_1953_num_42_1_2405 |journal=Journal de la société des américanistes |volume=42 |issue=1 |pages=127–134 |doi=10.3406/jsa.1953.2405}} Jorge Zevallos Quiñones (1941, 1946),{{Cite journal |last=Zevallos Quiñones |first=Jorge |date=1941 |title=Una nota sobre el primitivo idioma de la costa norte |journal=Revista Histórica |volume=14 |pages=376–379}}{{Cite journal |last=Zevallos Quiñones |first=Jorge |date=1946 |title=Un diccionario yunga. Mochica o Yunga |url=https://glottolog.org/resource/reference/id/156368 |journal=Revista del Museo Nacional |volume=15 |pages=164–188}} and [[Paul Kosok]] (1965),{{Cite book |last=Kosok |first=Paul |title=Life, land and water in ancient Peru |date=1965 |publisher=Long Island University Press}} whose wordlist contains a large amount of errors. Finally, the last rememberer of Mochica, Simón Quesquén (1918-1995), one of Rafael's sons, had recordings made of his speech in Mochica in 1974, the only ones known in existence.{{Cite journal |last1=Herrera Calderón (†) |first1=Américo |last2=Ziemendorff |first2=Michaela |last3=Ziemendorff |first3=Stefan |date=2019-06-30 |title=Grabaciones del extinto idioma mochica |url=http://journals.iai.spk-berlin.de/index.php/indiana/article/view/2579 |journal=Indiana |language=es |volume=36 |pages=77–108 |doi=10.18441/IND.V36I1.77-108}} == Names == Colonial sources record several designations for the language now generally known as Mochica: ''Yunga'', ''Mochica, Muchic''/''Muchik'', and occasional appellatives such as ''Pescadora''. Oré's ''Rituale'' refers to the "Mochica" language and also uses the phrase {{lang|es|Mochica de los Yungas}} ('Mochica of the [[Yungas]]').{{Cite book |last=de Oré |first=Luis Jerónimo |author-link=Luis Jerónimo de Oré |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QWK12GojzF4C |title=Rituale, seu Manuale Peruanum, et forma breuis administrandi apud Indos sacrosancta Baptismi, Poenitentiae, Eucharistiae, Matrimonij, & Extremae vnctionis sacramenta. Furthermore, nineteenth-century archaeology often grouped [[Sican culture|Sicán]] and [[Moche culture|Moche]] material into stages labeled "proto-Chimú" or "early Chimú", which reinforced the misattribution. Later archaeological and linguistic research clarified these associations and dissociated Quingnam from Mochica. April 2024}} == Revival == The Cultural Office of the district of [[Mórrope District|Mórrope]] has launched a program to teach the Mochica language in an effort to preserve the region’s ancient cultural legacy. The initiative has been well received by local residents and adopted by numerous schools. Additional cultural activities, such as the crafting of ceramics and decorated gourds (mates), have also been introduced as part of the revitalization effort.{{cite web |title=Lengua Muchik: Entrevista sobre su recuperación en Mórrope |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oBru1X3PDWo |url-status=dead |access-date=7 June 2025 |website=YouTube}} Previously considered a [[dead language]], Mochica is now taught in 38 schools and has around 80 teachers.{{cite web |date=December 24, 2018 |title=La lengua muchik ya tiene 80 muchik hablantes |url=https://larazon.pe/la-lengua-muchik-ya-tiene-80-muchik-hablantes/ |access-date=7 June 2025 |website=La Razón}} ==Phonology and orthography== The sounds of Mochica are not known with certainty due to the differing transcriptions used by different authors. In addition, the two primary sources on Mochica were recorded over 200 years apart, with significant phonetic changes having occurred during that time. === Vowels === ==== Carrera Daza (1644) ==== Carrera Daza distinguishes six vowels in Mochica, represented as {{Angle bracket|a, e, i, o, u, æ}}, with the latter sometimes being written as {{Angle bracket|œ}} in different editions of his grammar. This vowel is characterized as "begin[ning] as an ''e'' and end[ing] as a ''u'', in such a way that there are two vowels in one". A diacritic is used to indicate length, though it is mainly restricted to a few roots ({{Lang|omc|ûtzh}} 'big') and the ending {{Lang|omc|-ô}}, used in the [[genitive construction]]. The letter {{Angle bracket|i}} is sometimes used as a [[Palatalization (phonetics)|palatalization]] marker by Carrera Daza (e.g. {{Lang|omc|ñaiñ}} {{IPA|/nʲanʲ/}} 'bird' or {{Lang|omc|çio}} {{IPA|/sʲo/}} 'he, it'), and [[Diphthong|diphthongs]] did not occur in the Mochica of his time.{{Cite book |last1=Adelaar |first1=Willem F. H. |title=The languages of the Andes |last2=Muysken |first2=Pieter |date=2004 |publisher=Cambridge University press |isbn=978-0-521-36275-7 |series=Cambridge language surveys |location=Cambridge (G.B.) |pages=322}} ==== Middendorf (1892) ==== In contrast, Middendorf recognizes 17 vowels, including 11 plain vowels, two "impure" vowels, written as {{Angle bracket|ů}} and {{Angle bracket|ä}}, and four diphthongs. Middendorf admits that he was never able to correctly pronounce the impure vowels, but characterizes them similarly to the {{Angle bracket|æ}} of Carrera Daza. {{Angle bracket|ä}} is described with a very fleeting ''u'' sound, such that in rapid speech it would sound similar to {{IPA|[ɛ]}} or {{IPA|[e]}}. {{Angle bracket|ů}} is described as reminiscent of the diphthong {{IPA|/aʊ/}}.{{Cite book |last=Eloranta-Barrera Virhuez |first=Rita Silvia |url=https://www.lotpublications.nl/Documents/563_fulltext.pdf |title=Mochica: grammatical topics and external relations |publisher=Rijksuniversiteit te Leiden dissertation |year=2020 |isbn=978-94-6093-348-6}} ==== The sixth vowel ==== The vowel represented by {{Angle bracket|æ}} is hotly debated in the field of Mochica studies. As no sound recordings of Mochica exist, and because the existing descriptions are rather vague, the true phonetic value cannot be discerned and any interpretations remain completely hypothetical. One hypothesis is that the sixth vowel was {{IPA|/ɨ/}},{{SAPhon|Mochica|Mochica}} commonly found in [[Amazonian languages]]. Other hypotheses have given realizations of {{IPA|[ɵ, ø, ʉ, ɘʊ, ɘ, œy̯]}} and {{IPA|[ǝ]}}. ==== Comparison ==== A comparison table of the vowels as written in Carrera Daza and Middendorf is given below. {| class="wikitable" |- align="center" !Carrera Daza |a, â |e |i |o, ô |u, û |œ/æ |- align="center" !Middendorf |a, ā, ă |e (ē) |ī, (i), ĭ |ō, (o), ŏ |u, ū, ŭ |ä, ů |} ==== Table ==== Thus, a vowel system of Mochica would resemble the table below: {| class="wikitable" style="text-align:center" ! rowspan="2" | ! colspan="2" |[[Front vowel|Front]] ! colspan="2" |[[Central vowel|Central]] ! colspan="2" |[[Back vowel|Back]] |- !short !long !short !long !short !long |- ![[Close vowel|Close]] |{{IPA link|i}} |{{IPA link|iː}} | rowspan="2" |{{IPA link|ɨ}} ~ {{IPA link|ə}} {{Angle bracket|æ, œ}} | |{{IPA link|u}} |{{IPA link|uː}} |- ![[Mid vowel|Mid]] |{{IPA link|e}} |({{IPA link|eː}}) | |{{IPA link|o}} |{{IPA link|oː}} |- ![[Open vowel|Open]] | | |{{IPA link|a}} |{{IPA link|aː}} | | |} === Consonants === The orthography used for Spanish at the time of the writing of Carrera's grammar was very chaotic and inconsistent. One may therefore never be quite sure on the nature of consonants, especially sibilants, in Spanish colonial texts of the time. ==== Sibilants ==== The symbols used to represent Mochica [[Sibilant|sibilants]] in Carrera (1644) are {{Angle bracket|ç/z, s, x}} and {{Angle bracket|ss}}. The grapheme {{Angle bracket|x}} is described unanimously among Mochica scholars as representing {{IPAslink|ʃ}}. All but two authors coincide in their description of the [[phoneme]] represented by {{Angle bracket|ç}} or {{Angle bracket|z}}. The only sources to disagree are Stark (1968), which interprets them both as different [[Allophone|allophones]] of {{IPAslink|ʃ}}, being {{IPAblink|ɕ}} and {{IPAblink|ʑ}} respectively. Hovdhaugen (2004) interprets them as having a palatal pronunciation, which is represented as {{IPAslink|sʲ}}. Carrera (1644) explains the distinction between {{Angle bracket|s}} and {{Angle bracket|ss}} as "they {{Angle bracket|ss}} have to be pronounced between them both, hurting on the last one as in ssonto, amoss." The use of "hurting" is derived from Nebrija's ''[[Gramática de la lengua castellana]]'', who described consonants and vowels using this definition: "they were called vowels because they have voice by themselves without mixing with other letters, the others were called consonants because they cannot sound without hurting the vowels". Thus, combining the two descriptions, it may be inferred that {{Angle bracket|ss}} "sounded only when the second (last) {{Angle bracket|s}} would affect the contiguous vowel", representing a sound like {{IPAslink|s̺}} or {{IPAslink|s}}. ==== Digraphs and trigraphs ==== [[Digraph (orthography)|Digraphs]] and [[Trigraph (orthography)|trigraphs]] used in Mochica are {{Angle bracket|cɥ}}, {{Angle bracket|tzh}}, and {{Angle bracket|xll}}. The digraph {{Angle bracket|cɥ}} is derived from a normal {{Angle bracket|ch}} but with the {{Angle bracket|h}} inverted to represent the difference. Middendorf (1892) describes his corresponding sound, written as {{Angle bracket|c̓h}}, as similar to the German {{Angle bracket|tj}}. Hovdhaugen (2004) interprets it as {{IPAslink|ʈ͡ʂ}}, Stark (1968) as {{IPAslink|t̠ʲ}}, Torero (1997, 2002) as {{IPAslink|kʲ}}, Eloranta (2013) and Michael et al. (2015) as {{IPAslink|c}}, Cerrón-Palomino (1995) as {{IPAslink|ʨ}} and Adelaar as {{IPAslink|tʲ}}. The trigraph {{Angle bracket|tzh}} is described as representing a sound difficult to pronounce by Carrera: "These [words] one pronounces starting with T, hurting on the Z and on the vowel, that comes after H, so that it does not say ''cha'' but ''tzha''." He further describes the articulation of it as having the "tongue touch[ing] the palate next to the teeth". Middendorf describes it as similar to the German {{Lang|de|z}} {{IPAslink|͡ts}}. The trigraph {{Angle bracket|xll}} is, according to Carrera, articulated as "[t]he X preceding consonant has to be pronounced hurting between both in a soft way, attaching the tongue to the palate, in such a manner that the sound of the first letter, the vowel, may come out through one side and the other of the mouth". Stark (1968) identifies this sound as {{IPAslink|ɕʲ}}, Torero (2002) as a [[voiceless post-palatal lateral fricative]] {{IPAslink|𝼆̠}}, Hovdhaugen (2004, 2005) as {{IPAslink|ʂ}}, Adelaar (2004) as {{IPAslink|ɬʲ}}, and Salas, Eloranta and Michael et al. (2015) as {{IPAslink|ɬ}}. ==== Other consonants ==== The following consonants are unanimously agreed upon by all sources: * voiceless [[Plosive|plosives]] {{IPAslink|p}}, {{IPAslink|t}}, {{IPAslink|k}}; {{IPAslink|ʈ}} is added by Hovdhaugen to represent the digraph {{Angle bracket|tr}} * voiced plosive {{IPAslink|d}}, also interpreted as {{IPAslink|ð}} by Adelaar and Hovdhaugen, and {{IPAslink|d̪}} by Stark * [[Nasal consonant|nasals]] {{IPAslink|m}}, {{IPAslink|n}}, {{IPAslink|ɲ}}, {{IPAslink|ŋ}}, though {{IPAslink|ɲ}} is replaced by a pre-palatal nasal by Torero (2002) * the [[Rhotic consonant|rhotic]] {{IPAslink|r}}, an alveolar [[Trill consonant|trill]]; a tap {{IPAslink|ɾ}} is also added by Stark and Cerrón-Palomino * a labial [[fricative]], either {{IPAslink|ɸ}} or {{IPAslink|f}} * the palatal [[Semivowel|glide]] {{IPAslink|j}} * the [[Postalveolar consonant|postalveolar]] fricative {{IPAslink|ʃ}}, although {{IPAslink|çʲ}} is also given by Stark as an alternative to represent the grapheme {{Angle bracket|x}} * the postalveolar affricate {{IPAslink|tʃ}}, which is replaced by Stark with {{IPAslink|tɕ}} * the [[Lateral consonant|laterals]] {{IPAslink|l}} and {{IPAslink|ʎ}}; Torero adds {{IPAslink|ɭ}} and interprets {{IPAslink|ʎ}} as pre-palatal. {{IPA|/l/}} shifted to {{IPA|[x]}} around the 18th and 19th centuries.{{Reference page|page=46|pages=}} ==== Table ==== Michael et al. Further, it contains rare features such as: * a case system in which cases are built on each other in a linear sequence; for example, the [[ablative case]] [[suffix]] is added to the [[locative case]], which in turn is added to an [[oblique case]] form; * all [[noun]]s have two stems, possessed and non-possessed;{{Reference page|page=|pages=263–265}} * an [[active–stative language|agentive case]] suffix used mainly for the agent in passive clauses; and * a verbal system in which all finite forms are formed with the [[copula (linguistics)|copula]].Hovdhaugen, Even (2004). ''Mochica''. Munich: LINCOM Europa.{{Reference page|page=33}} ==Morphology== Some suffixes in Mochica as reconstituted by Hovdhaugen (2004): *sequential suffix: {{lang|omc|-top}} *purpose suffix: {{lang|omc|-næm}} *gerund suffixes: {{lang|omc|-læc}} and {{lang|omc|-ssæc}} *gerund suffix: {{lang|omc|-(æ)zcæf}} *gerund suffix: {{lang|omc|-(æ)d}} ===Nouns=== ==== Possession ==== Mochica maintains a distinction between [[Inalienable possession|inalienable and alienable possession]]. Inalienable nouns are divided into three [[Noun class|noun subclasses]], and alienable nouns into two, which can be distinguished from each other by their possesive prefixes. The former require a suffix when not possessed, and do not have a suffix when possessed. of Martínez Compañón === Mochica is attested in a 43-word list in a document referred to as the "plan" collected by Martínez Compañón between 1782 and 1785. The "plan" is part of a larger work, known as the [[Codex Martínez Compañón]], detailing life in colonial Peru.Martínez Compañón, Baltasar Jaime. 1985 [1782-1790]. ''Trujillo del Perú en el siglo XVIII'', vol. 2. Madrid: Ediciones Cultura Hispánica. The work also contains a number of watercolors, which were captioned by Martínez Compañón's personal secretary [[:es:Pedro Agustín de Echevarri|Pedro Agustín de Echevarri]], who presumably also wrote down the "plan". There are two copies of the "plan", one held in [[Bogotá]] and the other in [[Madrid]]. Both copies include 43-word lists for the [[Quechuan languages|Quechua]], Mochica (Yunga), [[Sechura language|Sechura]], [[Colán dialect|Colán]], [[Catacao dialect|Catacaos]], [[Culle language|Culli]], [[Hibito language|Hibito]] and [[Cholón language|Cholón]] languages, as well as Spanish. The Colán and Catacaos languages are generally subsumed under the name ''Tallán'', and they are closely related, probably dialects of a single language. The two versions of the "plan" have certain differences from each other, particularly in the spelling of the transcriptions. A number of diacritics are employed in the vocabularies. Their meaning is not elaborated upon in the "plan", although certain diacritics are employed in only some of the languages, and are apparently not merely decorative in purpose.
